safetyNote: Poisonous: do not eat this bolete. It can cause marked nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea; poisoning has also been reported after a cooked meal. If it may have been eaten, contact a poison centre or emergency medical service promptly.

sections.title: Satan’s bolete
sections.text: Rubroboletus satanas, formerly Boletus satanas, is a large stout bolete with a pale whitish to putty-grey cap, sometimes with faint olive or pinkish tones. The cap can reach about 25 cm across. Its pale cap is an important contrast to the red pores and yellow-red stem; red or blue bruising by itself is not enough to identify the species.

sections.title: Pores, stem and cut flesh
sections.text: The underside has tubes, not gills. Their pores begin yellow-orange, turn orange-red to red, and blue on handling; the tubes are yellow in section. The very thick, swollen stem is yellow near its top and pink to red lower down, with a fine red net. The pale cream to yellowish flesh blues slowly and often only weakly, especially in the cap and upper stem. The spore print is olive-brown.

sections.title: Habitat and comparison
sections.text: In Europe this bolete grows with broadleaved trees, especially beech and oak, in warm sites on calcareous soil, usually from summer into autumn. Other red-pored boletes can resemble it: some have a darker or pinker cap, different flesh colours or a stronger, differently distributed blue reaction. Old fruit bodies may smell unpleasant, but odour varies and is not a safe test.

sections.title: Poisoning
sections.text: The species causes a gastrointestinal poisoning syndrome with nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea. In a Swiss emergency-department series, patients were treated after eating specimens recorded as Boletus satanas, including a cooked meal. The short profile’s claim that poisoning occurs chiefly with raw or undercooked specimens should therefore not be read as a cooking recommendation. The mushroom must not be consumed.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The plate shows a whole stout bolete, a longitudinal section with pale flesh and a small area of blue bruising, the pale cap from above and the red-pored underside. The red net and pore colour are typical mature features; younger specimens may have paler pores.
